About

Research is the foundation of creativity and design.

Kehinde Arojojoye is a User Experience Designer who excels at performing the research necessary to maximize the quality of experience of all users by combining in-depth research with simple design that applies complex details. Kehinde believes that the right design can make users feel seen and understood, bringing them back to the site, and turning a user into a customer.

Kehinde has completed the UI/UX Bootcamp from the University of Maryland Global Campus. Kehinde holds a bachelor's degree for Information Science from UMD College Park.

When he is conducting user research, Kehinde can be found making music and art or playing soccer.

Work / Cortex

Cortex

A premium-subscription flow to motivate free users to become paid users.

01

Description of the Project

The brief was a "Media Company" scenario: design a path that leads both new and returning users toward subscribing to a premium tier. It's a UX problem as much as a UI one, since the interface has to make the upgrade feel earned.

My UX skills were tested through interviews, usability tests, and research into how industry leaders handle the same problem. My UI skills were tested through a style guide and wireframes, refined into a prototype across two rounds of testing.

02

My Role

I was the lead designer on this project, working solo. I owned research, UX, UI, and usability testing end to end, and a design mentor checked in for critique and direction at each phase.

03

My Team

This was an independent project. My "team" was one design mentor, who reviewed my work at each phase and pushed back on soft spots before I moved forward.

04

Problem

A media app gained a user base with a freemium model. Now, they needed a way to nudge free users into paying for the monthly premium subscription. This was to be accomplished using UX and UI.

05

Research

I studied industry leaders YouTube, Spotify, and Pandora, taking notes on how each one navigates users toward its premium tier. There's no single playbook: each company nudges users differently, so I wrote a competitive research paper scoring all three against the factors I thought mattered most.

Competitive research: scoring rubric and a close read of Spotify's premium flow.

06

Concept Sketches

Before any screen was drawn, I sketched the flow by hand, mapping every route a viewer could take from opening the app to hitting a wall that Premium solves, including the sign-in and payment detours.

07

Art Board

The name "Cortex" was chosen to signal intelligence and savviness, and that promise had to show up in the palette and type before a single UI screen existed. The palette leans on a confident green and a cool neutral grey, paired with a display face that has enough personality to carry the brand.

08

Low Fidelity Prototype

Low-fidelity wireframes were built in Figma to test the prototyping and flow of the screens. The cake needed to work well and be intuitive before icing could be put on top.

09

Usability Tests

Round one tested the low-fidelity prototype over Zoom against a script built to probe the most important features. The notes showed my wording needed to be clearer. Round two tested a higher-fidelity prototype and asked about visuals too, which pushed the direction toward something more restrained and closer to professional patterns.

10

High Fidelity

The final design carries the Cortex branding through custom art direction and type, in a modern UI language inspired by current trends like Apple's liquid glass. Premium prompts sit inside natural stopping points in the viewing flow rather than blocking the screen outright.

Walk through the full project in Figma

Open in Figma →
11

Insights

01

Free-tier quality signals premium value

Companies convince users to get the premium experience in different ways. Some are more forceful than others.

02

A name can carry the brand's promise

The product name "Cortex" was chosen deliberately to signal intelligence and savviness, setting the tone for the visual and interaction design before a single screen was drawn.

03

Modern UI trends move fast, and imitate the leaders

Studying pro interfaces on Mobbin, Behance, and Dribbble showed how quickly trends like Apple's "liquid glass" ripple across the industry, and how similar top-tier products end up looking.

＋

Learnings

The real lesson was about visual language more than UX. I understood the flows and the psychology well, but until I broke down reference patterns from professional interfaces line by line, my UI was trying too hard to be original instead of being clear.

Work / Havenly Homes

Havenly Homes

A home-buying app built to ease the pain of the housing crisis with simplicity and trustworthiness.

01

Description of the Project

The brief: design a prototype for an app that solves a real, specific problem, start to finish. I chose home buying, because so much of the process is opaque to first-time buyers, and shaped it into Havenly Homes.

UX skills were tested through interviews, usability tests, article research, personas, and red routes. UI skills were tested through wireframes and a style guide, refined into a prototype against real usability feedback.

02

My Role

I was the lead designer on this project, working solo. I owned research, UX, UI, and usability testing end to end, and a design mentor checked in for critique and direction at each phase.

03

My Team

This was an independent project. My "team" was one design mentor, who reviewed my work at each phase and pushed back on soft spots before I moved forward.

04

Problem

During the housing crisis we were experiencing at the time, the problem was finding a way to alleviate some of the pain through UI/UX.

05

Research

Research started with a screener survey to find the right participants, followed by an empathy map to understand what buyers say, do, think, and feel. Those four don't always agree, which is exactly why mapping them separately mattered. Interviews were then compiled into a persona and a set of prioritized user stories.

Screener survey, empathy map, persona, and prioritized user stories.

06

Concept Sketches

Early concepts were sketched by hand first, laying out the homepage and the buy, rent, and sell routes before touching Figma. Settling the structure early meant visual polish only started once the layout actually worked.

07

Art Board

A shared kit of components, including buttons, icons, and other common elements, kept the interface consistent as screens multiplied. A moodboard kept the photography and colour palette aligned throughout. The discipline of minimalism carried straight through. The user is able to process information easier since there is less thrown at them.

Component kit and moodboard, the shared visual language for every screen.

08

Low Fidelity Prototype

Wireframes translated the sketches into a testable structure: the tour-scheduling flow, a listing detail screen, and the homepage buy flow. All three were designed mobile-first, since a mobile layout expands cleanly into desktop but the reverse rarely works.

Low-fidelity wireframes: tour scheduling, listing detail, and the homepage buy flow.

09

Usability Tests

With wireframes in hand, I checked the priority tasks from the red routes against the built structure to make sure they stayed reachable in as few taps as possible. It was a quieter form of testing than a moderated session, but it kept scope honest before moving to high fidelity.

10

High Fidelity

Havenly Homes gives first-time buyers a mobile-first path through home search that mirrors the priorities set by the red routes. It's built around minimalism, so the app never throws more information at a buyer than the moment calls for.

Walk through the full project in Figma

Open in Figma →
11

Insights

01

The persona made needs concrete

Compiling interview data into a single average user turned scattered opinions into a clear list of needs to design for.

02

Hierarchy matters more than completeness

User stories showed that buyers want a lot of things, but only a few matter first. The rough draft needed to start with those and add detail later.

03

Designer knowledge isn't user knowledge

Because I built the site from the ground up, I understood it perfectly. But, users meet it for the first time, so I had to guide the user and make everything as intuitive as possible.

＋

Learnings

Designing from the ground up means I always know how Havenly Homes is supposed to work. Every user meets it cold though, with their own assumptions. My job was making the interface clear and intuitive enough to close that gap. I'd also change how I framed my early research, which chased the housing crisis in general instead of the buying experience specifically.

Work / George's Comics

George's Comics

A more engaging comic-book learning experience, designed around the client's vision of commerce, community, and education.

Explore the project deliverables in Figma

Open in Figma →
01

Bringing a comic-book vision to life

Our three-person team worked with client George Poulios to refine his comic-book website before its official release. The experience was built around three connected goals: commerce, community, and education. Users would be able to buy, sell, and trade comics; connect with other comic fans; and develop their writing and drawing skills.

Rather than starting from scratch, we reviewed the previous team's Figma files and the more up-to-date existing website, then identified the changes needed to bring the client's vision together.

02

Designer, collaborator, and note taker

I worked alongside a team leader and another designer. I also documented our meetings, capturing details about the client's goals and decisions so our team could translate his ideas into clear design changes.

Each designer took ownership of one of the three core areas. I chose Education because of my interest in writing and art and my experience with comic books.

03

Designing for learning, not competition

The client wanted the Workshop to feel like both a live class and a self-paced course, with a welcoming, after-school tone rather than academic language. He also wanted people to create comics together, share work with others, and take part in group writing sprints.

Through our conversations, we refined several ideas such as one unified flow instead of separate beginner and expert paths, a sharing-focused Gallery instead of a leaderboard, and access to both new and past assignments. We also aligned on green as the Education section's color and removing AI-generated art in favor of comic-related imagery.

04

Understanding the vision and education

George had already worked with previous bootcamp teams, and we received their Figma files alongside the more up-to-date website. Both were incomplete, and he wanted our team to make the final refinements before launch.

Through questions, we learned that he wanted a fun, specialized comic shop, not one that simply met the bare minimum. His larger vision brought together commerce, community, and education with a particular focus on reading, writing, and drawing. He hoped to eventually create a physical shop, but first wanted to perfect the online experience.

My focus became Education. The Workshop needed to feel like both a live class and a self-paced course, with welcoming, after-school language rather than an academic tone. George also wanted people to read comics, collaborate on stories and art, and take part in group writing sprints.

05

Splitting the work

With three members on the team, we divided the work so each designer could own one of the project's three core focuses. I chose Education because of my interest in writing and art and my experience with comic books.

We each created a page outlining the scope and timeline for our section and listing the final deliverables. This made responsibilities and expectations clearer while allowing each person to contribute unique ideas and move the work forward efficiently.

06

Drafting the user flow

With the information gathered from our conversations, I created a sketch of the revised user flow. I changed the language to feel more connected to comic books: Workshop became Training Room, Classroom became Studio, and Live Workshop became Mentor Sessions.

I also planned for the Training Room's secondary navigation to remain visible, added carousels to suggest more writing sprints and mentor sessions, and made the “View More” action more prominent. For the writing sprint, I explored letting users rearrange pages and add narration and dialogue.

07

Building the high-fidelity Figma files

After I presented the rough draft, George approved moving into the high-fidelity design. Since the previous team's Figma files were outdated compared with the live website, I used screenshots of the current HTML experience to recreate the screens in Figma, then applied the changes from my sketches.

I carried the green Education color through the buttons, replaced AI-generated art with imagery from a comic-book movie, and compared my screens with my teammates' designs to keep the experience consistent. Working in Figma helped me give the pages more personality and polish.

08

Ask questions until the vision is clear

The most valuable lesson from this project was understanding what the client wants. Asking as many questions as needed helped me build a clear picture of his vision and translate it into design decisions. Because there were no established target audience members to interview, our conversations with George helped us understand the details of his trailblazing idea.

Those questions helped the team refine features around community and learning, and create deliverables that both the client and the team could be proud of.
